result:
There is a quiet magic in the way autumn surrenders its trees to the wind. I notice it most on cool mornings, when the pavement wears a mosaic of amber, copper, and burnt orange. Each leaf carries a season’s labor—sunlight captured, rain absorbed, growth measured in slow increments. Now they fall, not in defeat, but in graceful release.

I’ve always found comfort in this transition. Summer’s urgency fades, replaced by something slower and more deliberate. The world exhales. Hearth fires crackle against the windowpanes. Birds gather in murmuring flocks, preparing for journeys I can only imagine. People pull heavy sweaters from storage and stir pots of soup, finding steady rhythm in the lengthening dark.

Time feels different in autumn. It doesn’t rush; it settles. Falling leaves remind me that letting go isn’t loss—it’s simply part of the cycle. Roots deepen beneath the first frost, waiting patiently for spring’s return. Standing under a branching canopy, I feel both remarkably small and profoundly connected, caught in the same natural turnover that has animated centuries of earth. This quiet surrender renews the spirit.

Maybe that’s why I love it. It asks nothing but attention. It gives back perspective. And when the last leaf finally detaches, spiraling down to join its fellows on the ground, I don’t mourn the bare branches. I trust the waiting. The seasons turn without apology, reminding us rest is as vital as bloom. Every ending carries the promise of renewal, written in frost and fading light.
